traveler: Mansa Musa (Musa I of Mali, called by Ibn Khaldun Musa ibn Abi Bakr)
title: Twelve Thousand Miles of Credit: the Mansa, the Crossing, and the Death Nobody Wrote Down
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kangaba, born into a collateral branch
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no source records the year or the place. The conventional c. 1280 is modern arithmetic worked backward from a disputed death date and a reported reign length. Kangaba stands here for the Keita heartland, not for an attested birthplace.
stops.campa: He is born into a collateral branch of the Keita, the house that took the Manding country two generations earlier at Kirina, where Sunjata broke Sumanguru and turned a confederation into an empire. Nobody writes down the day, and nobody writes down the village. The c. 1280 in every modern book is arithmetic run backward from a death date that is itself disputed. Ibn Khaldun, working from informants a lifetime later, calls him Musa son of Abu Bakr and leaves the filiation there; the pedigree that runs from Sunjata's brother through Faga Leye is a reconstruction laid over that one name.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Kirina, c. 1235, in the Koulikoro region, where the Keita imperial order begins
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', on the uncertainty of birth date and filiation
Ibn Khaldun's dynastic history, as summarized in the modern literature
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Kirina'

stops.name: Niani, the court they call only Mali
stops.date_confidence: traditional and disputed: older scholarship makes Niani the capital, and the Guinean-Polish missions of 1965 and 1968 found an Arab quarter, stone foundations, a mosque mihrab and royal walls there. Whether Niani or Kangaba held Musa's court is unresolved, and the date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: The mansa rules from a seat his own subjects do not trouble to name. Al-Umari's informants, asked what the capital is called, answer with the name of the kingdom: Mali. What he governs is not a bordered territory with surveyed provinces but a layered thing of subordinate kings, garrisons, wells and roads, and he holds it by holding the roads. Excavation on the Sankarani has turned up an Arab quarter, house foundations, a mihrab and the walls of a royal town. Is that his court, or somebody else's? Nothing in the ground answers the question, and the scholars have argued it since the digs of 1965.
suggested_refs: The excavated royal town at Niani on the Sankarani, Guinea
sources: Wikipedia, 'Niani, Guinea', on the excavations and on al-Umari's informants
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Bure, the gold in the gravel
stops.date_confidence: attested as a working medieval goldfield across the period; no source fixes a date or describes the crown's arrangements with the miners, and the date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: South and west of the court, on the upper Niger, men wash gold out of gravel and out of pits. The mansa does not own the seams. Mining communities and middlemen work them and move the dust north on their own account, and what reaches the crown reaches it as tax and tribute, not as production. He controls no part of the ground and taxes a commodity half the known world wants, at the point where the only road out of the goldfields runs through him. What the rate was, who collected it, and what a miner kept at the end of a season, no source records.
suggested_refs: The Bure goldfields of the upper Niger, the bullion base of the Mali empire
sources: Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali
Timothy Insoll, The Archaeology of Islam in Sub-Saharan Africa

stops.name: Bambuk, the field already going
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a correction to the popular account: Bambouk is attested as a major medieval goldfield, but wasteful working had already cut its productivity by the eleventh and twelfth centuries, two hundred years before Musa. Its share of his bullion is inference, not record.
stops.campa: Between the Senegal and the Faleme lies the older field, worked so long and so hard that its yield was falling before Musa's great-grandfathers were born. It still ships. The arithmetic that hands him every ounce of West African gold quietly assumes Bambuk was pouring at full strength in 1324, and the sources say it had been in decline for two centuries. Most of what goes north with him comes from somewhere else. How much from where is a question no medieval account was ever asked, and none of them volunteers an answer.
suggested_refs: The Bambouk goldfields between the Senegal and the Faleme, in decline from the twelfth century
sources: Wikipedia, 'Bambouk', on the reduced productivity of the goldfields by the eleventh and twelfth centuries
Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali

stops.name: The Atlantic shore, two thousand vessels
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction throughout. The story survives only in Musa's own words to an Egyptian official, relayed to al-Umari; no source names a departure point, and this pin near the Senegal mouth is geographic convention. No archaeology anywhere confirms a landfall, and the date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: His predecessor did not believe the ocean had a far side that could not be reached. He sent two hundred vessels west with supply boats behind them, and one came back. Its captain said the fleet had run into a river in the middle of the open sea, a current pulling hard, and had gone into it and not come out. The mansa fitted out two thousand more, appointed Musa his deputy, and sailed with them. Nothing of that fleet was seen again. Everything known about any of it is a few sentences Musa spoke in Cairo years afterward, to a Mamluk official who wrote them down.
stops.quote: Yes, O Sultan, we traveled for a long time until there appeared in the open sea [as it were] a river with a powerful current. Mine was the last of those ships. The [other] ships went on ahead but when they reached that place they did not return...
stops.quote_source: The returning captain's report, as told by Mansa Musa to Ibn Amir Hajib in Cairo in 1324 and recorded by al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar
suggested_refs: Al-Umari's Cairo interview material on the Atlantic expeditions of Musa's predecessor
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, via Ibn Amir Hajib, in the translation quoted at Wikipedia, 'Abu Bakr II'
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Niani, the deputy becomes mansa
stops.date_confidence: conventional, not attested: 1312 is worked backward from a death date and Ibn Khaldun's figure of a twenty-five-year reign. A death in 1332, which is seriously argued, would put the accession nearer 1307.
stops.campa: The sea keeps the king and the deputy keeps the throne. There is no coronation in the record: no acclamation, no oath sworn under a tree, no date anyone set down at the time. Ibn Khaldun, told a century afterward that the reign ran twenty-five years, gives the modern historians their only lever, and they work backward from a death that is itself disputed to an accession that is therefore disputed too. What survives in place of a date is Musa in Cairo twelve years later, answering a Mamluk official who asked him how the office had come to him.
stops.quote: He left me to deputize for him and embarked on the Atlantic Ocean with his men. That was the last we saw of him and all those who were with him, and so I became king in my own right.
stops.quote_source: Mansa Musa to Ibn Amir Hajib, Cairo, 1324, in al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar
suggested_refs: Nawal Morcos Bell, 'The Age of Mansa Musa of Mali: Problems in Succession and Chronology'
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, quoted at Wikipedia, 'Abu Bakr II'
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', citing Ibn Khaldun's reign-length figure

stops.name: The royal seat, the death of Kanku
stops.date_confidence: late tradition, dated here only to place it before the pilgrimage. The story appears in West African chronicle material compiled around three centuries after Musa and in no near-contemporary source; it is carried as penitential legend, not biography.
stops.campa: A horse rears, or bolts, and kills his mother Kanku in the courtyard of his own house. He goes to Mecca, the story runs, out of remorse for it. No Arabic writer of his own century mentions the accident, or his mother, or any motive of penitence at all; the episode surfaces in Timbuktu chronicles put together long after the Mali empire had ended, in a genre that likes a king to have a sin behind his piety. It is not biography. It is the only story anyone tells about his mother.
suggested_refs: The seventeenth-century Timbuktu chronicle tradition, Ta'rikh al-Sudan and Ta'rikh al-Fattash
sources: Later West African Arabic chronicle tradition, c. seventeenth century, as characterized in the modern secondary literature
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: The royal seat, the caravan sets out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1324 for the pilgrimage; the month of departure is not recorded. The figures given for the caravan are described in the sources themselves as rhetorical rather than statistical.
stops.campa: The numbers the chroniclers give are not counts. Upwards of twelve thousand enslaved people, eighty camels carrying gold dust, a road reckoned at some two thousand seven hundred miles before Egypt: these are the numbers of a genre, written to say enormous rather than to say how many. Something enormous goes north out of the Manding country all the same, provisioned for a year, moving at the pace of loaded camels through country where water is a political fact and every well belongs to somebody who must be dealt with before anyone drinks.
suggested_refs: The Mamluk-era Arabic accounts of the caravan of 1324 and their conflicting figures
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', giving 'upwards of 12,000 slaves' and 80 camels and calling such numbers rhetorical rather than statistical
Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold, 'Mansa Musa's Hajj to Mecca'

stops.name: Mema, the western staging ground
stops.date_confidence: route reconstruction: no member of the caravan left an itinerary. Mema's place in the sequence is inferred from trade geography, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The road out runs first through Mema, where the caravan is still in watered, governed, tributary land, moving between towns whose chiefs owe the mansa grain and men. Water here is given or bought, not fought for. Beyond it lies the crossing, which is why a pilgrimage out of Mali is a matter of state and not of piety alone: it takes an army's logistics to move a king to Mecca and bring him home again. This flooded delta country is also where Sunjata's family sheltered during the wars with Sumanguru, before there was an empire for anyone to inherit.
suggested_refs: The Mema region of the inland Niger delta, refuge of the Keita during the Sumanguru wars
sources: Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold, tour of Mansa Musa's hajj route
Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali

stops.name: Walata, the gate of the empire
stops.date_confidence: route reconstruction for Musa specifically. Walata's role as the southern terminus of the Sijilmasa road is attested, and its replacement of Aoudaghost dates to the beginning of the thirteenth century, a century before this caravan rather than recently. No source places Musa in the town.
stops.campa: Walata is where the empire stops and the desert road starts. It had taken over from Aoudaghost a century before as the southern end of the great route running down from Sijilmasa through the salt mines, and everything going north to the Maghreb and everything coming south into Mali passes through here and is counted. The Massufa Berbers hold the wells and the road; the mansa holds the town, and neither arrangement is written down anywhere. Mauny reckoned the place at two or three thousand people. No source puts Musa inside it.
suggested_refs: Oualata, southern terminus of the Sijilmasa-Taghaza caravan road
sources: Wikipedia, 'Oualata', on the route from Sijilmasa through Taghaza and on Mauny's population estimate
Northwestern University, Caravans of Gold

stops.name: Taghaza, the houses of salt
stops.date_confidence: route reconstruction for this caravan. Taghaza's construction out of salt slabs, and the fourfold price increase on the road south, are attested from Ibn Battuta a generation later, not for 1324.
stops.campa: Deep in the sand there is a settlement built out of the thing it sells: walls of cut rock salt, roofs of camel hide, no other material within many days' travel in any direction. Two slabs are loaded to a camel going south, and by the time those slabs reach the markets of Mali they are worth four times what they cost here. Nobody lives at Taghaza who has not been made to. The gold going north crosses the salt coming south here, in the same yards, and has done for centuries. Ibn Battuta saw the salt houses a generation later and wrote them down; for 1324 there is only the road and the trade on it.
suggested_refs: The salt workings of Taghaza in the Taoudenni region, cut and carried south by caravan
sources: Wikipedia, 'Taghaza', citing Ibn Battuta for the salt-block construction and the fourfold price increase

stops.name: Tuwat, the chain of oases
stops.date_confidence: route reconstruction from standard trans-Saharan trade geography; not attested for Musa's caravan, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The wells of the Tuat oases come up out of the sand in a chain, date palms over them, each one a market and a garrison and a place where duty is paid. This is the desert's other half, the settled half, where a caravan can buy instead of ration, and where a party this size has to be fed by somebody who was warned in advance. From here the roads fork, north toward the Maghreb or east along the oases toward Egypt. Which fork this caravan took, and how many of the twelve thousand were still walking by the time it reached the fork, no source says.
suggested_refs: The Touat oasis complex and its wells on the trans-Saharan routes
sources: E. W. Bovill, The Golden Trade of the Moors
Route reconstruction from standard trans-Saharan trade geography; not independently attested for 1324

stops.name: Ghadames, perhaps
stops.date_confidence: flagged uncertain in the research itself, which carries this leg only as a perhaps. One plausible waypoint among several possible crossings, with nothing to decide between them.
stops.campa: Some reconstructions run the caravan through Ghadames, the old walled well-town on the Libyan road, and some do not. The honest state of the evidence is that between Walata and the pyramids of Giza there is nothing but silence and trade routes: no letter, no chronicle entry, not one member of the party who set down where they slept, what they paid, or how many died on the way. The route on any map of this journey is drawn from where caravans generally went. Generally is not a source.
suggested_refs: The Ghadames oasis on the Libyan caravan road toward Egypt
sources: Route reconstruction, carried in the research dossier itself as an explicit 'perhaps' and not confirmed elsewhere

stops.name: Giza, three days among the pyramids
stops.date_confidence: attested: the three-day camp at Giza and the crossing of the Nile on 19 July 1324 are given in the Arabic tradition. The date here is the start of the camp, counted back three days from the crossing.
stops.campa: Before entering Cairo the whole train halts for three days on the west bank, among the pyramids, in sight of a city of a couple of hundred thousand people. It is a formal pause rather than a rest. Baggage is sorted and the gifts are counted out, and the protocol of the entry is settled: who rides where, and what is given to whom in what order. Egypt has never received an embassy of this kind and does not yet know what is camped outside it. On the fourth morning they cross the river.
suggested_refs: The pyramid field at Giza, campsite of the Malian caravan in July 1324
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa': camped for three days by the Pyramids of Giza before crossing the Nile into Cairo on 19 July 1324

stops.name: Cairo, across the Nile into the city
stops.date_confidence: attested: 26 Rajab 724 AH, 19 July 1324.
stops.campa: He comes over the river into the Mamluk capital on the twenty-sixth of Rajab, and the chroniclers who see him agree on one picture: young, brown-skinned, good-looking, well made. He tells the officials who question him that he has conquered twenty-four cities with their surrounding districts. Egypt writes it down, and what Egypt writes down is the whole surviving life. Two of the three notices of his face are so alike that they may be one report told twice rather than two men looking. No Malian record of this journey exists, or of any other.
stops.quote: young man, brown-skinned, with a pleasant face and handsome appearance
stops.quote_source: Ibn Habib al-Halabi, on Musa's appearance in Cairo, 1324
suggested_refs: The Mamluk chancery and chronicle notices of the Malian embassy of 724 AH
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', quoting Ibn Habib al-Halabi and Ibn Kathir, and giving the claim of 24 cities conquered
al-Maqrizi, quoted in Ki-Zerbo, ed., UNESCO General History of Africa, vol. IV, abridged ed., p. 59

stops.name: The Citadel, the prostration refused
stops.date_confidence: attested through al-Umari, reporting Ibn Amir Hajib; the day within July 1324 is not fixed. This stop uses the Cairo Citadel, al-Nasir Muhammad's seat, where the other Cairo stops use the city pin.
stops.campa: Brought before al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, he is ordered to kiss the ground, and refuses. How may this be, he asks. Pressed, he finds the way out himself: he goes down, and says as he goes down that the obeisance is to the God who made him and not to the man on the dais. Neither man is made a vassal by it. The sultan comes partway off his seat and has him sit alongside, and robes, horses and gifts follow. The wording of the refusal reaches us through al-Umari; the excerpt that carried it into English is now a dead link, and the reading needs checking against the standard translation.
stops.quote: I make obeisance to God who created me!
stops.quote_source: Mansa Musa at the Cairo Citadel, 1324, in al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar; the online excerpt carrying this wording now returns a dead link and the reading should be checked against Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History
suggested_refs: The Citadel of Cairo, seat of al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, via Ibn Amir Hajib
Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, the standard translation, not directly reachable in this pass
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Cairo, the gold goes out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the spending and for the fall in the gold price; the day is not recorded. The strong version, a twelve-year depression caused by this visit alone, is contested by modern work on Mamluk exchange rates.
stops.campa: He gives. Every emir and officeholder of the court takes a load; the markets take the rest. Before he arrived a mithqal of gold fetched at least twenty-five silver dirhams in Cairo and usually more. After him it dropped below twenty-two and stayed there. Al-Umari, writing a decade later from men who had handled the transactions, says it had not recovered in twelve years. Economists reading the Mamluk price series accept the shock and doubt that one caravan is the whole explanation for a decade of it.
stops.quote: This man flooded Cairo with his benefactions.
stops.quote_source: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar; the online excerpt carrying this wording now returns a dead link and the reading should be checked against Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History
suggested_refs: Warren C. Schultz's survey of Mamluk exchange rates and the gold-price question
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, in Levtzion and Hopkins 2000, p. 271, cited via Wikipedia, 'Musa I of Mali'
Wikipedia, 'Shihab al-Umari'

stops.name: Cairo, what the retinue bought
stops.date_confidence: attested: al-Maqrizi records the purchases and the six-dirham fall in the dinar rate; the day is not recorded.
stops.campa: The spending is not all alms. Al-Maqrizi sets down what the mansa's people did with their gold in the Cairo markets, and it is buying: Turkish and Ethiopian slave girls, singing girls, garments, on a scale that moved the exchange rate by itself. The caravan that came north with twelve thousand enslaved people in it goes home having bought more. He is in Cairo three months and the buying goes on through them. Al-Maqrizi sets the figure down without comment: the rate of the gold dinar fell by six dirhams on those purchases.
stops.quote: the members of his entourage proceeded to buy Turkish and Ethiopian slave girls, singing girls and garments, so that the rate of the gold dinar fell by six dirhams
stops.quote_source: al-Maqrizi, on the Malian party in the Cairo markets, 1324
suggested_refs: The Cairo slave markets of the Mamluk period and the Malian purchases of 724 AH
sources: al-Maqrizi, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Mali Empire', 'Height of power'

stops.name: Cairo, the question about the daughters
stops.date_confidence: near-contemporary but secondhand, through Ibn Amir Hajib to al-Umari, and the day is not recorded. The episode is not in the standard encyclopedia article and must be cited to Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History.
stops.campa: An Egyptian religious official tells him that what he does at home is unlawful: a king may not take an unmarried subject's daughter to his bed. He is surprised by it. Not even for kings, he asks. He is told not even for kings, and is reported to have stopped. The exchange reaches us through an Egyptian official and an Egyptian encyclopedist, and it records royal sexual coercion in Mali as a matter of routine while arranging for Egyptian law to be the thing that ended it. Whether it ended is not something a man in Cairo was in any position to know.
stops.quote_source: Mansa Musa in Cairo, 1324, reported by Ibn Amir Hajib to al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar
suggested_refs: Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, the al-Umari section
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, via Ibn Amir Hajib, in Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History; not directly reachable in this pass

stops.name: Cairo, out with the pilgrim caravan
stops.date_confidence: attested: 28 Shawwal 724 AH.
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of Shawwal he goes out with the official caravan, three months after arriving. The Egyptian court sends him off equipped, and the sultan has given him a residence in the city; the accounts of what was given are nearly as careful as the accounts of what was spent. Three months have been long enough to make him a fact of Egypt's economy and a line in its price history, and he leaves it as a creditor. The chroniclers give the day of departure and nothing about the mood of it. The date is 18 October 1324.
suggested_refs: The Mamluk state pilgrim caravan, the Darb al-Hajj al-Misri, leaving Cairo in Shawwal 724
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', giving the departure on 28 Shawwal 724 AH, 18 October 1324

stops.name: Aqaba, the road into Arabia
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only: no source describes this leg or names a crossing point. The pin is Aqaba on the Egyptian pilgrim road, the conventional Mamluk-period route, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Egyptian pilgrim road runs from Cairo across Sinai to the head of the gulf and then south down the Arabian side, wells and stations laid out and garrisoned by the Mamluk state for exactly this traffic. Nothing in the record says which stations he used, how long he took, what the crossing cost him, or whether the Mamluk escort stayed with him past the frontier. For a journey retold everywhere as one of the most spectacular ever made, the middle of it is blank. Between the Nile and the Hijaz the record is empty.
suggested_refs: The Darb al-Hajj al-Misri, the Egyptian pilgrimage road and its stations
sources: Standard Mamluk-period hajj geography; not stated for Musa's caravan in any source consulted, and flagged here as reconstruction

stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested that Medina was among the cities of his pilgrimage; the order relative to Mecca is not fixed in the sources and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He visits the Prophet's mosque and the tomb inside it. The sources mention it and move on: one clause folded into a general account of devotions, no scene, no words, no gift itemized. It is a fair measure of what the Arabic writers were interested in. A great deal of this pilgrimage was recorded because it was expensive, and the parts that were only religious pass in a phrase. Alms are given here as at Mecca. Who received them, and how much, nobody troubled to set down.
suggested_refs: The Prophet's Mosque at Medina, visited on the pilgrimage of 724 AH
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', naming Medina among the cities of the pilgrimage

stops.name: Mecca, the circuit of the House
stops.date_confidence: attested that he performed the hajj in the season of 724 AH; the day of arrival is not recorded and the date orders the segment. The recruitment of four sharifs is late West African tradition, not near-contemporary testimony.
stops.campa: He circles the House. Whatever else the journey is, this is the thing it was undertaken for, and it is the one part of it that requires him to be indistinguishable from every other man in the courtyard: the same white cloth, the same circuit, no retinue, no dais, no gold. He makes ties here with scholars and with sharifs of the Prophet's line. Later West African tradition says he talked four of them into coming home with him, a thousand mithqals each and a place at his court.
suggested_refs: The Kaaba and the Masjid al-Haram, station of the pilgrimage of 724 AH
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'
Broad consensus of the Mamluk-era Arabic accounts of the hajj of 724
Later West African tradition on the four sharifs, flagged as late and possibly stylized

stops.name: Arafat, the standing
stops.date_confidence: presumed, not attested: no source describes Musa at Arafat. The standing on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijja is what makes a hajj a hajj, so a completed pilgrimage implies his presence. The date is calculated from the hajj season of 724 AH.
stops.campa: On the plain below the mount the pilgrimage arrives at the hour without which it has not happened. Everyone stands from noon until sunset. No chronicler puts the mansa of Mali on this plain, because it did not occur to any chronicler to say so; they agree he completed the hajj, and completing it means he stood here through one afternoon among a hundred thousand strangers. Two pieces of unsewn cloth, bareheaded, in the heat, with nothing about him to tell him apart from any of them.
suggested_refs: The plain of Arafat and the standing of the ninth of Dhu al-Hijja
sources: Standard hajj ritual geography; presumed for Musa and not independently attested in any source consulted

stops.name: Masjid al-Haram, the fight in the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: attested in the tradition on the hajj of 724 AH; the day is not given, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Malian pilgrims and Turkic pilgrims come to blows inside the sanctuary itself, in the season, in front of the assembled Muslim world. The accounts do not say what started it or how far it went. What they say is that Musa went to his own people and talked them out of it. They obey him in a foreign country, under provocation, thousands of miles from anywhere he can enforce a thing, and the fighting stops. Nobody wrote down what he said to them, or what the Turkic pilgrims did next.
suggested_refs: The Masjid al-Haram in the hajj season of 724 AH and the quarrel between the Malian and Turkic pilgrims
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Mecca, al-Sahili takes service
stops.date_confidence: attested that Musa met and recruited Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Sahili on the pilgrimage; the exact place within the Hijaz and the date are not fixed, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Sahili of Granada, poet, jurist and secretary, about thirty-four years old, meets the mansa somewhere in the Hijaz and takes service with him. He is an Andalusi of the kind the western Mediterranean was then exporting in quantity: educated, mobile, looking for a patron with money. He will ride south with the caravan, build at the court, live another twenty-one years in the Sudan and die at Timbuktu. Maliki jurists join the party too. The pilgrimage is also a hiring fair.
suggested_refs: John Hunwick, 'An Andalusian in Mali: A Contribution to the Biography of Abu Ishaq al-Sahili', Paideuma 36 (1990)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Abu Ishaq al-Sahili'
Hunwick, Paideuma 36 (1990), named as the modern authority on the recruitment

segments.name: The Road Home and the Debt

stops.name: Suez, the return goes wrong
stops.date_confidence: attested that the returning caravan suffered a serious setback near Suez, with pilgrim deaths and lost supplies; the date within 1325 is not fixed.
stops.campa: Somewhere near Suez the return goes wrong. Pilgrims die, supplies are lost, and the accounts are brief and unspecific: no cause, no numbers, no names. What is clear is the position it leaves him in. The party that came north as the wealthiest thing anyone in Egypt had ever seen comes back through the desert short of everything, having given away in three months what took a year to assemble, with thousands of miles of road still ahead and a court to be provisioned at the far end of it.
suggested_refs: The return leg of the Malian caravan and the losses reported near Suez in 1325
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Cairo, borrowing back what he gave away
stops.date_confidence: attested for the borrowing and for the sales at a loss; the day is not recorded. The 50,000 dinar loan from the Banu al-Kuwayk is Ibn Khaldun specifically, not al-Umari, and whether it was ever repaid is disputed across the sources.
stops.campa: He comes back to a city he has personally made cheap. Cairo's merchants, who profited buying from him on the way out, now profit selling to him on the way back, and the Malians unload goods at half what they paid for them. Ibn Khaldun records a loan from the merchant family of the Banu al-Kuwayk, fifty thousand dinars, at the rate a borrower with no choice accepts. He is said to have surrendered the house the sultan gave him against the debt. Whether any of it was ever repaid, the sources do not agree.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Dawadari, Kanz al-durar wa-jami' al-ghurar, vol. 9, on the Malian sales at a loss
sources: Ibn Khaldun on the Banu al-Kuwayk loan, as summarized in Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Gao, the princes and the dispute
stops.date_confidence: contested on every point. The hostage story comes from seventeenth-century Timbuktu chronicles, three hundred years later, and not from Ibn Khaldun; the Gao tradition instead calls Ali Kulun the first ruler of the Sunni dynasty and a rebel against Malian hegemony, and dates Gao's incorporation into Mali to the end of the thirteenth century, which would make a conquest by Musa in 1325 impossible.
stops.campa: Coming home east of the Niger bend he is said to have taken or retaken Gao through his commander Saghmanja, and to have carried the Songhay ruler's sons, Ali Kolon and Sulayman Nar, back to be raised at his own court. Every element of that sentence is contested. The chronicles that supply the names were compiled three centuries later. Another tradition has Gao under Malian control since before Musa was born, and remembers Ali Kulun not as a hostage at all but as the man who rebelled and founded a dynasty on it.
suggested_refs: Ta'rikh al-Sudan and Ta'rikh al-Fattash on Ali Kolon and Sulayman Nar
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gao', calling Ali Kulun the first ruler of the Sunni dynasty and a rebel against Malian hegemony, and dating Malian control to the end of the thirteenth century
Ibn Khaldun on the conquest of Gao, as summarized in the modern literature

stops.name: Gao, the mosque that carries his name
stops.date_confidence: traditional attribution: Gao has a fourteenth-century mosque known as the Kankou Moussa Mosque, distinct from the later Askia tomb-mosque, but the naming is later memory and no contemporary inscription ties it to Musa. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: A fourteenth-century mosque at Gao carries his mother's name and his own, Kankou Moussa, and tradition hands him the founding of it as part of the building that follows the pilgrimage. He has come back from Mecca with jurists, an architect and the standing of a king who performed the hajj under the eye of the caliph's own city, and he spends that standing on mosques. The building is real and fourteenth-century. No inscription on it names him, and the name it carries was attached later, by people who wanted the mosque to have been his.
suggested_refs: The Kankou Moussa Mosque at Gao, fourteenth century
sources: Wikipedia, 'Gao', naming a fourteenth-century Kankou Moussa Mosque distinct from the Askia tomb

stops.name: Djinguereber, the mosque at Timbuktu
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the creation is attributed to Musa in 1325 with the building dated 1327. The fabric standing today has been rebuilt many times since. Hunwick's work shows al-Sahili is firmly attested only as designer of a royal audience chamber, not of this mosque.
stops.campa: The great mosque of Timbuktu goes up on the mansa's order, mud and timber, and is rebuilt so often across the following six centuries that nothing of the first fabric can be pointed at. The story that the Andalusi al-Sahili designed it single-handed, that a man from Granada brought architecture to the Sudan, is a favorite of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries and does not survive examination. Timbuktu had builders and a building tradition before he got there; what Musa supplied was money. Hunwick, going through the sources, found al-Sahili firmly attested as the designer of one building, and it was not this one.
suggested_refs: The Djinguereber Mosque of Timbuktu, attributed to Mansa Musa, built 1327
sources: Wikipedia, 'Djinguereber Mosque', on the 1325 attribution, the 1327 building, and Hunwick's finding on al-Sahili
Wikipedia, 'Abu Ishaq al-Sahili'

stops.name: Sankore, the quarter of the scholars
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction and correction: the Sankore mosque's own sourced history does not mention Musa at all, crediting early funding to a Tuareg woman of the Aghlal tribe, and the scholarly institution flourished later under the Songhay Askias. The date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: The story that he founded a university at Timbuktu is not true in any sense the word will carry. The learning that made the name famous grew over the following two centuries, mostly under rulers who came long after Mali had lost the city, and what Musa did was pay for buildings and import jurists. He did not found Timbuktu either. The town was there before him. As for the mosque of Sankore, the record credits its early funding to a Tuareg woman of the Aghlal, whose name it does not give.
suggested_refs: The Sankore Madrasah, Timbuktu, and its Aghlal patroness
sources: Wikipedia, 'Sankore Madrasah', crediting early funding to a Tuareg woman of the Aghlal tribe and making no mention of Musa

stops.name: The royal seat, the domed audience chamber
stops.date_confidence: attested by al-Umari for the building itself and for the price of 12,000 mithqals. No source dates it and no source resolves where the capital was, so both the pin and the date are placeholders following the disputed identification of the royal seat with Niani.
stops.campa: Al-Sahili's documented work is not a mosque. It is a room. Of everything attributed to Musa, this is the one building a near-contemporary source can be said to have had described to him in detail: al-Umari, who is careful and frequently skeptical, sets down a square chamber under a plastered dome, worked over in colored arabesques, built at the court for the mansa to receive people in. Musa pays twelve thousand mithqals for it, about fifty-one kilograms of gold. The windows may have held glass. Al-Umari does not commit himself on that.
suggested_refs: Al-Umari's description of the domed audience chamber built by al-Sahili at the Malian court
sources: al-Umari, Masalik al-Absar, in Levtzion and Hopkins, Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History

stops.name: Timbuktu, the Mossi raid and the rampart
stops.date_confidence: attested that Mossi forces took Timbuktu and that Musa recovered it and ordered a rampart and a stone fort; the year 1330 is conventional and not firmly fixed.
stops.campa: Forces out of the Mossi kingdoms come north, take Timbuktu and hold it for a time. The empire that appears in the Egyptian accounts as an unlimited quantity of gold appears here as the other thing it also was, a state with a long frontier and neighbors who crossed it. Musa takes the city back. He orders a rampart thrown around it and a stone fort raised inside, in the same decade the mosque goes up. The year is conventionally given as 1330 and is not firmly fixed.
suggested_refs: The rampart and stone fort ordered at Timbuktu after the Mossi occupation
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'

stops.name: Tadmekka, the gold and the glass
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: excavation at Essouk-Tadmekka documents gold-processing technique for the period of Musa's empire, and nothing ties the work to him personally. The pin is the medieval site northwest of Kidal in the Adrar des Ifoghas, and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Northeast in the Adrar des Ifoghas, at the town the Arabic geographers call Tadmekka, artisans refine gold using glass to draw off the impurities, a technique the excavators found in the ground and in no text at all. This is the work underneath the story. Gold does not arrive in a Cairo market; it is washed out of gravel, refined at a furnace, and walked north on a camel by people the Arabic writers never name and the excavators know only by what they left in the ground. Nothing found at Essouk ties any of it to Musa personally.
suggested_refs: Sam Nixon's excavations at Essouk-Tadmekka and the glass-assisted refining of gold
sources: Archaeological findings at Essouk-Tadmekka, cited in the research dossier and requiring Nixon's excavation reports for the refining detail

stops.name: Tlemcen, the embassy that outlived him
stops.date_confidence: attested in Ibn Khaldun, though the same passage elsewhere confuses Musa's son with his brother. The death it implies, around 1337, competes with an alternative around 1332 that is still seriously argued.
stops.campa: The Marinid sultan Abu al-Hasan Ali takes Tlemcen, and Mali sends congratulations across the desert, king to king. The Marinid reply travels the same distance back and arrives to find somebody else on the throne. That gap, the width of a courier's round trip, is the single strongest piece of evidence anyone has for when Musa died, and it comes from a passage that elsewhere cannot keep his son and his brother apart. It is not evidence of a date. It is evidence that he died inside the time it takes a letter to cross the Sahara twice.
suggested_refs: Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-'Ibar, on the Malian embassy to Abu al-Hasan Ali at Tlemcen
sources: Ibn Khaldun, as summarized in Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'
Wikipedia, 'Tlemcen', for the Marinid capture

stops.name: The royal seat, a death with no grave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: 1337 is Levtzion's reading and the most commonly given, with about 1332 seriously argued against it. Neither the place nor the cause nor the month of death is recorded anywhere. This pin is a placeholder for the royal seat and not an attested site of death.
stops.campa: He dies. That is the whole of it. No source describes an illness, a deathbed, a funeral, a burial or a tomb, and no tomb has ever been found. Al-Umari, writing close to the event, reports only that Musa had meant to hand the kingdom to his son and go back to Mecca to live out his life there, and that he did not manage it in time. He leaves no grave. Levtzion reads the year as 1337 and most books follow him; about 1332 is still seriously argued, and there is nothing in the sources to decide between them.
stops.quote: was an upright man and a great king, and tales of his justice are still told
stops.quote_source: Ibn Khaldun on Mansa Musa, written some fifty years after his death
suggested_refs: Nehemia Levtzion's reconstruction of the Malian succession chronology

stops.name: The royal seat, Maghan succeeds
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction from Ibn Khaldun's reign lengths, which are internally inconsistent and are precisely why the death date cannot be fixed. The month is invented to order the segment.
stops.campa: His son Maghan takes the throne and holds it about four years. Almost nothing else is remembered of him. Those four years of a man's life survive in the record chiefly as an interval of stated length, a number historians add and subtract trying to work back to the year his father died. The numbers refuse to close. Ibn Khaldun's figures for Musa, Maghan and Sulayman cannot all be true together, and the passage that supplies them mixes up the son with the brother.
suggested_refs: Nawal Morcos Bell, 'The Age of Mansa Musa of Mali: Problems in Succession and Chronology'
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa'
Ibn Khaldun's reign-length figures, as reconstructed by Bell

stops.name: The royal seat, the standard he set
stops.date_confidence: attested: Ibn Battuta reached Mali under Musa's brother Sulayman, whose reign runs c. 1340 to c. 1359, with some scholars arguing 1341 to 1360, and recorded the comparison. He never met Musa, who had been dead about fifteen years. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Fifteen years after the death a Moroccan traveler arrives at this court, is given a reception he thinks cheap, and writes down what the people around him evidently already thought: that the reigning mansa is a miser and the previous one was not. Ibn Battuta never met Musa and did not need to. By 1352 Musa's generosity had become the measure other Malian kings were held against, his own brother included, and the man applying the measure was a foreigner who had been in the country a few months.
stops.quote: a miserly king from whom no great donation is to be expected
stops.quote_source: Ibn Battuta on Mansa Sulayman, Rihla, c. 1352
suggested_refs: Ibn Battuta's Rihla on the court of Mansa Sulayman, c. 1352
sources: Ibn Battuta's Rihla, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Mansa Sulayman'

stops.name: Paris, the map that gave him a face
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Catalan Atlas, Bibliotheque nationale de France MS Espagnol 30, sheet 6, conventionally dated 1375 and attributed to Cresques Abraham of Majorca. Some scholars now place its making in the late 1370s or early 1380s. The pin is the Richelieu site, where the manuscripts department holds it, not the place of production.
stops.campa: Forty years after his death, in a Majorcan workshop, a Jewish cartographer draws the interior of Africa and seats a crowned Black king in it, holding a lump of gold the size of his fist, with a caption naming him. Nobody in Majorca had ever seen him. The image is what the gold did to Europe's picture of the world, drawn by men working from merchants' reports out of the Maghreb. Cartographers kept putting him on maps for nearly two centuries afterward: Angelino Dulcert in 1339, Jacopo Russo still in 1525.
stops.quote: This black Lord is called Musse Melly and is the sovereign of the land of the black people of Gineva (Ghana). This king is the richest and noblest of all these lands due to the abundance of gold that is extracted from his lands.
stops.quote_source: Legend on panel III of the Catalan Atlas, Majorca, conventionally dated 1375
suggested_refs: Catalan Atlas, BnF MS Espagnol 30, sheet 6, Departement des Manuscrits, Richelieu
sources: Wikipedia, 'Catalan Atlas'
Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', on Dulcert 1339 and Russo 1525, neither inspected directly in this pass

stops.name: Kangaba, the name becomes a road
stops.date_confidence: oral tradition, recorded in the twentieth century; the date marks the recording rather than the tradition. The Fajigi identification is reported in the standard summaries. A further merger with Sunjata's general Fakoli could not be confirmed and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: In Manding oral tradition pieces of him detach from the biography and attach to a culture hero called Fajigi, father of hope, who goes east and brings back what a people needs. The griots keep him that way, not as a chronology but as a departure and a return. Everything datable that is known about Musa was written in Egypt, by Egyptians, for Egyptian readers. What his own country kept was a story about a man who went away and came back carrying something.
suggested_refs: The Fajigi cycle in Mande oral tradition
sources: Wikipedia, 'Mansa Musa', on Fajigi, translated as father of hope

stops.name: Djinguereber, the tombs broken
stops.date_confidence: attested: between about 30 June and 10 July 2012 Ansar Dine attacked ten monuments in Timbuktu, destroying nine mausoleums and damaging the Sidi Yahya mosque. Two tombs at Djinguereber itself were destroyed on 1 July with hoes, pick-axes and chisels, though damage to the mosque fabric was minimal.
stops.campa: Six hundred and eighty-five years after the mosque was raised, men with hand tools break the tombs at its foot because they hold the veneration of saints to be idolatry. The building itself is barely touched. Timbuktu had been a World Heritage site since 1988 and on the danger list from 1990 to 2005; it went back on in 2012 and has stayed there. One of the men responsible pleaded guilty at The Hague and was sentenced to nine years, the first conviction anywhere resting on the destruction of cultural heritage alone.

stops.name: Cairo, the number put on him seven centuries later
stops.date_confidence: a modern commercial claim, not a historical one: the 400 billion dollar figure comes from a celebrity net-worth website with no medieval price basket behind it. Dated here to the September 2021 comparison the site itself makes.
stops.campa: A website that estimates the fortunes of living celebrities gives him four hundred billion dollars and calls him the richest human being who ever lived, ahead of Elon Musk. There is no arithmetic under the number. There is no medieval accounting to convert, no price series, no inventory, nothing but chroniclers writing the word enormous in the vocabulary of their genre. What actually happened in this city in 1324 is measurable: the mithqal fell from twenty-five dirhams to under twenty-two and did not come back up. That is the only figure in the whole story that anyone recorded at the time.
suggested_refs: Celebrity Net Worth, 'Mansa Musa Net Worth', the source of the 400 billion dollar figure
sources: celebritynetworth.com, fetched and confirmed, comparing the figure to Elon Musk's reported net worth of September 2021
